speechtext:
Perhaps corporations, as my friend said. It can bypass the duly elected local governments which historically have received equalization payments. It can do it for no other reason than to buy votes in a partisan manner, which I would not put past the Liberal party because of its traditional program over the years. I have only to ask people in Newfoundland and Quebec. They will confirm that this practice has been only too common in those two provinces.
We are a federation. We are supposed to try to reach a consensus before doing things. As my leader said, before acting unilaterally we must try as much as possible to have the consensus of all provinces and the federal government. I looked at the equalization proposal and I followed the conference across the street. Only one province supported the proposal in section 31 whereas nine provinces supported a different proposal. I have a copy of it here, but time does not permit me to read it. That proposal refers to the fact that Parliament and the Government of Canada are committed to making equalization payments to ensure provincial governments have sufficient revenues to provide levels of public services at reasonably comparable levels of taxation. It lists in more succinct detail the regulations that would govern the payment of equalization payments in the country. I say to the House, and through the media to the people of Canada, that we must take a look at section 31. It is not enough to endorse it in principle. Indeed we may be endorsing the Liberal party or any other government buying votes in provinces and going over the heads of the legislatures, instead of endorsing something on which all the provinces are agreed.
The third matter I should like to raise is an objection to sections 20 and 23 dealing with the official languages of our country. I Find a bit of a double standard. Section 20 refers to two languages in federal institutions and parliament. When we

October 7, 1980
The Constitution
get to determining whether or not numbers warrant, we find out that parliament will determine what the numbers are, whether numbers are warranted for bilingual services, whether numbers are warranted for French in the nine provinces that are predominantly English, whether numbers are warranted for English in Quebec.
Then we go on to section number 23. 1 support the fact wholeheartedly, as the Minister of Justice knows, of making sure that there are schools for Anglophones in Quebec and Francophones outside Quebec. We find out when we talk about where numbers are warranted, it is not the provinces, the provincial legislatures, or the people elected-and education is provincial-but it is left to the courts. 1 do not accept that double standard in federalism.
1 see, Mr. Speaker, you are signalling me to sit down. 1 see it is five o'clock and 1 did want to speak for five or six minutes more, if 1 could continue. With your permission, I will. If not, 1 will come back at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for your co-operation. I have no gratitude at all for the co-operation that is extended to me from the other side of the House. I was prepared to agree to the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) continuing and having that few minutes extended beyond six o'clock. I am very surprised that the government should say it is not going to be obstreper-
October 7, 1980

ous this early-this is day two of the resumed session. It is already being obstreperous by not allowing the extra few minutes to the discussion of a very important bill.
As the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Collenette) has said, 1 did stand down on the day the House rose and I hoped, even then, that there would be some give on the government's side to introducing sane, sensible, meaningful proceedings in this House so that, as was promised by the government of the Thirty-first Parliament, all government members' bills would have two hours of debate and would be able to be voted upon-not talked on, but voted upon-as to whether they should go to committee. But I see that there has been no move to have the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization reconvened so that we can have meaningful debate on private members' bills. Therefore, 1 shall proceed with the discussion, my opening remarks on the second reading of this bill. I do hope it will not be talked out today. That is why I felt a failure of the Chair to see the clock at six for those few minutes might permit the government member to sit down-because 1 am sure one of them is planning to talk it out-so we could agree to have this matter go to committee for discussion, and come back to this House for a free vote. I mean a free vote, like one of those freedoms that this government claims to be putting into the charter of freedoms and rights.
Mr. Speaker, I am committed to the notion that man as a rational being is responsible for the acts he commits. The purpose of this bill, as will be seen on page 1A of the bill-

subsubtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: Will it be a free vote in your own party?

subsubtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Yes, there will be a free vote in this party, too. That is an undertaking given by the leader of this party a good many years ago, and he stands by it.
The purpose of this bill is to restore the death penalty for first degree murder and high treason while substituting a more humane mode of execution for hanging, because I abhor this notion that the television and press have of putting a noose on the screen and front pages to depict the sentence of death. The punishment for serious narcotic offences would also be stiffened to the point of the death penalty for persistent repeaters.
It may come as a surprise to some members of the House that the death penalty is on the statute books of Canada. Section 75 of the Criminal Code, which deals with piracy, indicates quite clearly that anyone who, in the commission of a piracy, for which offence he would be liable to imprisonment for life, murders or attempts to murder another person, or does any act that is likely to endanger the life of another person, shall be sentenced to death. That is the penalty. It is still on the statute books.
It is the purpose of the bill that if, under a certain set of circumstances, a rational being kills another, he has forfeited his right as a law-abiding citizen and the law should take its course. The course I propose is the death penalty. I say the murderer has demonstrated his unwillingness, or his unreadiness-it is a matter of degree-to live by the laws that others
Capital Punishment
are prepared to obey, for one reason or another. He may demonstrate this unwillingness by carrying a deadly weapon and by using it.
The decision in the first place to carry a death-dealing weapon, be it a knife or a gun, is in itself a rational act and a preparation for a commission, in certain circumstances, of a crime. Although it could be a poker game for which this individual is setting out, it is more likely that in such circumstances he is on serious business, either to rob a bank or to hold up someone. This person carries with him a death-inflicting weapon and seems prepared to use it. If the individual had no weapon but his body and hands and was prepared to use them in such a way as to extinguish the life of another, the consequences are the same and the full effect of the law should be applied. My bill says that that full effect is death.
It should be clear that the intent of my bill is not vengeance but deterrence. The argument over deterrence will be heard interminably. I insist that it is a matter of belief. Those who believe that there is no deterrence are entitled to their opinion, but I feel that they should allow those who believe that the death penalty is a deterrent the entitlement of their opinions, and I would like to see a free vote on that matter.
With regard to statistics, how can we compare known statistics on those who have not drawn back with those who have drawn back at that fatal moment? They are not going to admit that they have drawn back. They are ashamed, thoroughly ashamed, of what they did and they do not want it known that they drew back because of a deterrent, but they did. On a statistical plane, I insist that there is no real valid means of comparison. So I insist that it is a matter of faith or belief that there is a deterrent in the presence of a death penalty on the statute books.
There are those, of course, who use the argument that it is abhorrent to take life. I abhor those who would take life out of a whim, fear or desperation, and without a fair and impartial trial. They are the judges and they take the life. Those are the ones whom I abhor. My concern is for the innocent victim. I can think of the many police officers who have in the performance of their duty lost their lives. I can think of a particular case which occurred within the last two or three weeks in my part of the world, I regret to say, in which an officer suffered death in the performance of his duty. He was just behind the counter of the police station. He left not only his wife, but a child and another child yet unborn. These are the people whom the law should protect.
Has rehabilitation proven its case? I suggest that the death penalty has proven its case very simply because the murderer is not able to commit a second murder. There are those who say they do not, but they do if we are to believe the press. I have before me a press clipping from April which describes the incident of a man who was being held in a triple killing. They do repeat the offence. They may not have been caught the first time. What about that creature-and I cannot think of a better word-in Chicago who went around enticing women

October 7, 1980
Capital Punishment
into the bushes and murdering them out of hand? That man has forfeited any right he had to live in a civilized society. In another case a killer from Repentigny escaped on July 13, 1980, while he was being taken on a visit, presumably as a rehabilitation exercise, to Les Floralies in Montreal. He escaped, and stabbed a man.
What does this bill contain? Its provisions are broad and the crime is specific. There is provision for appeal and commutation. But once all recourse to a second or third look is exhausted, the sentence is final.
The bill speaks of treason. I do not think there should be any question in the world but that someone who has committed a treasonable act has forfeited the right to live in that society. Those who kill officers of the law and prison guards in the performance of their duties, such as in prison breaks, and those who kill fellow inmates should face the death penalty. If death occurs in the course of a highjacking, kidnapping or forcible confinement, rape, or attempt to commit rape or indecent assault, then the death penalty should be there to be used.
Finally, where there is a second offence of murder, once under the provisions of the current law and once under the provisions of this bill which might become law, the death penalty should be considered. I suggest that those who traffic in drugs in large quantities and who are apprehended committing that crime more than twice have forfeited their right to live in the society of this world, not just in the society in which that crime was committed.
This is a controversial bill and there is no question about it. But let us face the controversy and let the bill go to committee and emerge for a free vote.
1 suppose one should not really deal with polls and percentages, but they exist nonetheless. The Gallup poll shows that 82 per cent of the people are in favour of the death penalty. My own poll in my own riding shows that 85 per cent of the people there are in favour of the death penalty. 1 have here another poll which was taken rather hastily one day by a radio station. All of the people in that poll supported the idea of at least some categories of murder being subject to the death penalty. I have another clipping which tells of a retired official from the Solicitor General's office who left his duties because he found that the members of Parliament were not addressing the real problems of crime. That clipping was found in The Globe and Mail of July 5, 1980.
There are those who would rather stay in prison than die because there is a chance of getting out. That is true. Here is a recent account of a convict who was given the option of life in prison, or death. He chose death. So I suggest that we proceed with our debate. I urge members on all sides of this House to allow this matter to come to a vote so that it may go to committee and be discussed at greater length, so that the issues can be examined in depth and detail, and so that it can come back to this House for a free vote.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon.
member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) has presented his reasons for putting forward Bill C-215, in a very articulate and very reasoned manner. But many aspects of the bill trouble me. The title of this bill is the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1980. The explanatory note is far more serious, and it is the principle and assumptions upon which Bill C-215 is based that concern me.
The explanatory note reads as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to restore the death penalty for first degree murder and high treason, while substituting a more humane mode of execution for hanging. The punishment for serious narcotics offences would also be stiffened, to the point of the death sentence for persistent repeaters.
In discussing this bill it is necessary to cover some territory which has been explored many times in this House of Commons with regard to similar pieces of legislation. I believe this is because the suggestion of the hon. member is not new. At the same time, the arguments for and against capital punishment are not new and so I should like to spend a short time reviewing the recent history of capital punishment in Canada.
On July 14, 1976, by a free vote of 130 to 124, this House abolished the death penalty for all crimes under the Criminal Code. The then Bill C-84 culminated a trend toward abolition which began in common law countries such as Canada, over a century ago. The criminal law of England introduced the "Bloody Code" to Canada which, in 1763, called for death as the penalty for over 200 crimes. Later, between 1859 and 1865, the extent to which the death penalty applied in Canada was narrowed, so that capital punishment became applicable only for murder, treason, and rape.
By the late nineteenth century, reforms on the application of the death penalty were progressively introduced into Canadian law. Following World War II, Canada moved legislatively to narrow the crimes for which capital punishment could be applied-following the lead of the United Kingdom.
After a long process of review-including the joint parliamentary committee in 1953-which witnessed a trial ban which maintained the death penalty for murders of police and prison guards, the death penalty was abolished for all crimes.
Outside of Canada, the scope of application of the death penalty has been progressively restricted in law. As recently as April, 1980, the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe adopted, by a wide margin, a resolution and recommendation favouring the abolition of the death penalty in all 21 member states of the Council of Europe.
In Canada and elsewhere in the world, the death penalty has been increasingly de-emphasized as a judicial instrument. A 1962 United Nations report concluded as follows:
The abolition or suspension ... of the death penalty docs not have the immediate effect of appreciably increasing the incidence of crime.
This is an empirical judgment: one which the author of Bill C-215 has not disputed.
But let me ask, Mr. Speaker, what kind of evidence can be brought forward in support of Bill C-215? What sorts of arguments can be asserted at this time which would lead this House to reopen a debate on the merits of capital punishment?
October 7, 1980

Perhaps it would be that the rate of homicide has increased. If our post-abolition experience in Canada had shown a disproportionate rise in the murder rate, which could be ascribed to abolition, then I could understand hon. members wishing to embark on a renewed debate on capital punishment.
Let us look at the evidence, Mr. Speaker. Allow me to refer you to the August, 1979, Statistics Canada publication entitled, unfortunately, "Homicide Statistics". Tables 1 and II of that document detail the situation with respect to homicide for the past several years.
Table 1 deals with homicide "incidents" which are distinguished from homicide "offences", which are detailed in Table II.
"Incidents" are defined as every single event in which homicide is committed.
"Offences" are defined as the total number of homicide victims in a given year.
Using either of these definitions, the 1978 rates for homicide in Canada were the lowest since 1974. The 1978 figures, as we are all aware, are the latest available on this subject.
The total rate of homicide incidents in 1974 was 2.46 per 100,000 population in Canada. The rate in 1975 went up to 2.77. In 1976, the year of abolition, the rate dropped to 2.66. In 1977, it rose marginally to 2.72. Then, in 1978, it fell again to 2.62.
Exactly the same pattern existed in the case of homicide offences. The 1974 rate of 2.67 was followed by a rise to 3.07 in 1975. This dropped to 2.89 in 1976, marginally rose to 3.03 in 1977, and finally in 1978 dropped to 2.80.
The 1978 murder incident rate of 2.35 per 100,000 population was the lowest since 1974. Similarly, the 1978 murder offences rate of 2.51 was also the lowest since 1974.
The principal conclusion which I would suggest we can draw from this data is that there is absolutely no evidence that the abolition of the death penalty for Criminal Code offences in 1976 has led to a disproportionate increase in the murder rate in Canada. In fact, as I have demonstrated, there has been a levelling off of that rate. The issue of changing murder rates in Canada cannot lead us to reconsider the question of abolition in this House.
Another point that I should like to raise with regard to the deterrent effect of capital punishment refers to the most recent information that I have available to me, which is an article in today's Globe and Mail. This deals with a study done in the United States regarding the deterrent effect of capital punishment by a sociologist at the University of California, Mr. David Phillips. The article reads as follows:
Executions of convicted killers deter other murders for no longer than two weeks, says a new statistical study.
David Phillips concluded from a three-year research project that the homicide rate drops during the week of a highly publicized execution and during the following week.
But Mr. Phillips, a sociologist at the University of California at San Diego, found that the murder rate then begins rising. "Within five or six weeks of a publicized execution, the drop in homicides is cancelled by an equally large rise in homicides," he wrote.
Capital Punishment
So, Mr. Speaker, this new evidence, which is the latest evidence, takes into consideration all previous data that has been available. I do not know the statistical validity of this study, but if it is the latest information we have we will have to go with it until we can examine it more closely. Being the latest study, it indicates to me that there is no evidence that there is a permanent or long-lasting deterrent effect from capital punishment when it is used in a country as a means of punishment.
A second issue which concerns me is clause 6 of Bill C-215. This clause provides, in part, for the re-introduction of former Criminal Code provisions instructing a judge to seek the recommendations of a jury as to clemency.
The amendment to section 670 of the Criminal Code provides for a judge to put a question to a jury in the course of which jurors are told that if they make a specific recommendation with respect to commutation, such a recommendation will be drawn to the attention of the Solicitor General and will be given "due consideration by the Government of Canada".
If you read this part of clause 6 with the subsequent amendment to section 671 which states, "would allow commutation to life imprisonment only where a majority of the jury so recommends", major problems become apparent.
Under the wording of Bill C-215, it is entirely possible to foresee a situation in which five members of a jury recommended positively for commutation, while the other seven jurors made no recommendation at all. Under Bill C-215 the cabinet would be prevented from even considering commutation of such a death sentence, because the amendment to section 671 of the Criminal Code forbids such consideration except in cases where "a majority of the jurors who found the person guilty of the offence recommended in favour of commuting the sentence". Surely this outcome cannot be considered just or reasonable.
The wording in Bill C-215 is inadequate since it gives members of a jury no indication whatsoever that their failure to make a recommendation would have the mandatory effect of sending an individual to his death without the possibility of cabinet review.
Nevertheless, even if this fatal weakness were remedied in Bill C-215, it seems to me that the bill places an intolerable burden upon a jury by giving them the unprecedented power to remove the discretion of the governor in council even to consider cases for commutation.
There are absolutely no criteria in Bill C-215 to guide or limit the absolute discretion of a jury to make a clemency recommendation. Bill C-215 also has the effect of widening the scope of the application of the death penalty. Not only is the sentence of death to be imposed in cases of planned and deliberate murders, or murders of police officers and prison guards, but it is also to be imposed in cases of death caused by a person while committing other offences. These can include aircraft highjacking, kidnapping, rape, attempted rape and indecent assult, to name but a few.

October 7, 1980
Capital Punishment
To make my point, allow me, Mr. Speaker, to refer to the amendments to the Narcotics Control Act suggested in clause lOof Bill C-215.
Presently, there is a maximum of life imprisonment for trafficking or possession for the purpose of trafficking, and there is a mandatory minimum seven-year term for importing or exporting.
The bill we are considering would establish as a judicial formula such things as the following: a mandatory minimum seven-year term for first offences; a mandatory minimum fourteen-year term for second offences and a mandatory death sentence for third offences.
Already, the seven-year term currently in law has been vigorously criticized by the Canadian Bar Association and by some judges. They feel it is too harsh. To replace the seven-year term with the formula set forward in Bill C-215 is completely intolerable. Bill C-215 would widen the scope of mandatory minimum sentences and provide for even harsher mandatory minimums, up to and including a sentence of death. In my opinion, this is unthinkable.
It seems to me there are but two reasons why anyone could put forward a bill which would bring back the death penalty. The first is the deterrent effect. In other words by having the death penalty on the statute books there would be fewer murders per 100,000 population in the future than in the past. 1 think the statistical evidence indicates that this is not the case in Canada both before and after capital punishment was abolished. In my view, the evidence does not support the deterrent effect, or at least the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) has not presented statistical evidence which would support his position and lead those who believe in the deterrent effect to support the bill.
The second reason one could put forward for bringing forward capital punishment is simply a desire for vengeance. I fear a situation where a civilized nation institutionalizes vengeance in its Criminal Code or in its criminal system. I think a system of government, a societal system, which builds upon itself or builds within itself a code of violence, begets violence.

speechtext: We have got it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
speechtext: I think that a situation where criminals are treated with violence leads to violence. 1 think that over time as a result of abolition of capital punishment we will find that because we do not institutionalize violence in our system in this way, we will probably wind up-I certainly hope this will be the case-with a fewer, rather than a greater, incidence of murder and such previously classed capital crimes. I hope that is the case. The evidence before me indicates some tendency in the direction I suggest. I will certainly want to watch that very carefully to see if that trend continues in the future. That is my hope, and until such other evidence can be brought to my attention, I hope that we will go no further in considering this legislation.

I turn now to consideration of the subject itself. The hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) has asked what are the priorities of this party. That includes the present leader of the Conservative party, 1 am pleased to say.
I might also point out that while the Conservative party was in government it took absolutely no steps whatsoever in the direction suggested by my hon. friend. 1 am pleased to note that. 1 am pleased to note that the initiative my hon. friend appears to be putting forward was in no way seen as a priority by the government his party formed for a short period of time in this country.

speechtext:
I also point out that at this particular moment it is divisive, and it would be destructive to embark again on a lengthy parliamentary debate on this subject. More than 100 members of Parliament took part in the debate in 1976 on this subject. I suggest we should be getting on to far more important issues at this time, issues which affect the people of Canada such as those I referred to earlier, rather than spending valuable parliamentary and committee time debating this issue. This issue should be allowed to remain dead.
What are some of the concerns we have with this bill? My friend from Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) said, and 1 certainly accept his statement, that he is not motivated by vengeance. He said he is motivated by deterrence. Surely there is some obligation on my friend to provide evidence that the measures he is proposing would in some way deter the crime of murder. No evidence has been submitted by my friend to suggest that if we stick needles in people and kill them, that will somehow deter the commission of the offence of murder.
Capital Punishment
If my friend is concerned about deterrence, rather than suggesting as he does in his bill that the method of execution would be by intravenous injection of sodium thiopentol, an anaesthetic which in sufficient dosage leads directly to unconsciousness and death, he should be proposing public hangings or perhaps public stonings which would have a far greater deterrent effect.
Why should we be sticking needles in people behind closed doors if we are concerned about deterrence? Rather, 1 suggest my friend should adopt the example of civilized countries such as Iran which have more open forums in which to stone and otherwise indicate their disapproval of various offences which are deemed to be capital in that country.
I would also point to some of the types of punishment which have been meted out in the past which have not in any way helped to deter the crime of murder and to some of the other crimes which have been capital offences in the past. In the past in countries such as the United Kingdom, the following have been used and have failed as deterrents. We have seen burning at the stake, boiling in oil and water, iron coffins, burying alive, breaking on the wheel, drawing and quartering, decapitation. My friend behind me says don't give them ideas, there might be another bill coming.
We have also seen impaling, hanging, crushing, flaying, shooting-maybe it should be retroactive-exposure to insects, poisoning, throwing to animals, stoning, drowning, torturing, electrocution, asphyxiation, crucifixion, mayhem, which is the amputation of one or both legs. All of these have been used in the past in an attempt to deter and all have failed.
Why should it be suggested by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich that sticking a needle in somebody behind closed doors will deter someone from committing the various offences which he would make capital? If someone is contemplating cold-blooded murder, surely he will not say to himself, "Well, I only face 25 years behind bars, so that's no problem". The reality is that they do not think about the penalty. Most think that they are too smart to get caught or are acting in a moment in which their emotions are governing, and certainly they are not acting rationally.
There are a number of other concerns we have with this bill. For example, in no way will this lead to an improvement of our criminal justice system and to a reduction in the number of murders in Canada. Instead, we should be looking at a number of other more positive and constructive measures. We should be looking at better trained, better deployed and better equipped police. We should be looking at more effective gun control, particularly hand gun control; preventive, rather than reactive police work, and more effective correctional programs for juveniles and adults. The resources presently put into juvenile programs when dealing with juvenile delinquents are miserably inadequate. We should be improving them substantially.
We should be looking at more effective and economic programs to remove the causes of crime and improve treatment for alcoholics and drug addicts. In other words, we should be attempting to prevent murders in this country by

October 7, 1980
Capital Punishment
effective programs rather than dealing after the fact in a manner which will not in any way reduce the number of murders. As has been suggested by the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), that merely sets a bad example in which the state is emulating the very act which it is condemning. The state is merely repeating that act.
There are those who seek to glorify or make martyrs of themselves. If the crime of murder were punishable by death, this would contribute to those individuals who seek the glory; the Gary Gilmours of this world who seek the publicity and exposure they would get in such a case.
Recently in one of our newspapers there was a letter to the editor headlined "A standard of humanity". I draw this to the attention of all hon. members as being a very vivid and graphic example of one of the reasons why we believe on this side of the House that this bill is a mistake. This letter was written by the widow of Sir Christopher Ewart-Biggs, a former British ambassador to Dublin. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich may be aware that Sir Christopher Ewart-Biggs was assassinated by the IRA. This letter was written by his widow, Lady Ewart-Biggs, following the assassination. I quote:
As capital punishment will be coming up soon for debate in the Commons, I am sure that some readers will welcome the use of your columns to express their views.
I would point out in explanation that the subject of capital punishment was recently debated in the U.K. Parliament. A motion in that Parliament to restore capital punishment was overwhelmingly defeated. The letter continues:
I look at this issue from a practical and moral viewpoint. Is hanging a deterrent to killing and is it morally defensible that the community should be empowered to decide on whether one of its members lives or dies?
Statistics convince me that the threat of execution does not deter the potential murderer. This leaves the moral standpoint. In my view it should be the responsibility of a civilized society to contain the destructive elements within it without resorting to similar methods. This whilst striving through social reform to eradicate the root causes of crime and violence. We must judge the criminal, condemn him, isolate him-but not emulate him.

On another aspect, and one which touches me deeply. It is felt that certain categories of murder justify the supreme penalty more than others. Murder through terrorist action is deemed one. Again, from both practical and moral viewpoints, this is to me indefensible. Society cannot degrade its own behaviour to match that of a terrorist.
It must, within the limitations imposed by a democratic state, wage continual war against the terrorist and strive to protect the community from his action.
I am convinced that the execution of a terrorist-thus making him a martyr- would infinitely enrich his cause. Many would rally with renewed vigour to fill his place. His supporters, sharing his contempt for human life, would in retaliation make further reprisals.
Surely the arguments which I have put forward can be shared by every sane, civilized, and compassionate human being.
As I say, that was written by the widow of Sir Christopher Ewart-Biggs, who was brutally assassinated by IRA terrorists. If any member of our community were in a position to wreak vengeance or in any way suggest that capital punishment is a deterrent, I suggest that a woman such as Lady Ewart-Biggs would have done so.
A former leader of the Conservative party, the late Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, had a story about the alleged deterrent effects of capital punishment. 1 should like to quote it because I know members of his party would be interested in this story, and I know that perhaps after hearing it they would want to change their views on this important subject. Mr. Diefenbaker said as follows:
My great-grandfather saw a boy hanged in Upper Canada for picking pockets in 1837. I think the boy was 17 years of age and everybody gathered for the public execution.
Those Scottish people in North York turned out in large numbers.
There was a great celebration, and during the ceremonies of the execution, four of them had their pockets picked, which just indicates the argument that the fear of capital punishment will greatly reduce the number of offences is not completely tenable, or indeed tenable at all.
That illustration, as I say, was from the distinguished lawyer and former leader of the Progressive Conservative Party.
There are other problems inherent in this bill and one of them is, of course, the fact that we have seen traditionally in this country, and in other countries, that the enforcement of capital punishment is very selective in nature. The reality is that it is not the rich who hang; in fact, it is the poor who hang. I would like to quote from a former warden of Sing Sing prison who has seen a lot of convicts come and go, Lewis E. James. He said as follows:
Not only does capital punishment fail in its justification-
That justification allegedly is deterrence.
-but no punishment could be invented with so many inherent defects.
It is an unequal punishment in the way it is applied to the lich and to the poor. The defendant of wealth and position never goes to the electric chair or to the gallows.
Juries do not intentionally favour the rich, the law is theoretically impartial, but the defendant with ample means is able to have his case presented with every favourable aspect, while the poor defendant often has a lawyer assigned by the court.
We have seen once again selective enforcement of the law, a law which obviously in its ramifications is very serious. We have also seen historically documented cases of errors made, of innocent people who have been executed by the state. Surely if members on this side of the House are concerned about the preservation of human life they would not want to bring into existence a punishment which has the possibility of taking innocent human lives.
1 should like to point to a couple of examples. One is cited in the Ottawa Citizen of May 20, 1976 relating to a man who spent seven years in jail for a murder which, ultimately it became clear, he had not committed. Another person confessed to the murder and showed by conclusive proof that indeed he was the person who had committed the murder. Had
October 7, 1980

the condemned man been executed, it would have meant an innocent life taken.
In concluding let me say that this is an issue which touches many people in Canada and on which many organizations and individuals have genuine differences of view. I would like to close by quoting from one important organization in this country, the Canadian Catholic Conference of Bishops. That Canadian Catholic Conference of Bishops has resolved that it is in favour of the abolition of capital punishment in Canada. At the same time it urged the government to move to bring about the reforms which are required in our penitentiary system and in all areas of justice. I am pleased that the Catholic Church has taken such a courageous stand on this important question. I suggest at this time that to embark once again upon a divisive and destructive debate of this nature when there are so many other important issues facing the people of Canada would be a very serious mistake. Mr. Speaker, I believe in capital punishment, the death penalty, in the case of a murder of a human being that has been deliberately planned and carried out and the person is found guilty without any shadow of doubt.
When we are young we are punished if we do something wrong; if we do something even more wrong we are punished more severely, yet people today are saying that when we commit the ultimate crime of killing another human being we should not then receive the ultimate punishment.
I think capital punishment is a deterrent. It is utterly impossible to determine how many people were not killed because of the fear of death. The argument against that is rather void. In my view the fact that people fear death makes this a realistic deterrent.
The death penalty is an effective tool that pinpoints law and order. The abolitionists appear to have no objection to punishing a child for stealing or a grown-up for rape. Why then in the logical order of things do we not go the rest of the way and exact the death penalty for those who commit the worst possible crime, the killing of another human being?
Violent crime is becoming all too rampant across Canada. The elderly and women are afraid to walk outside after dark in some of our cities. Boys and girls are being murdered by animals, as I call them. We then put the convicted in jail, provide them with education, the best of TVs and food and we keep them there for the rest of their lives. One of these days all these criminals being kept in these prisons will get together and commit a terrible crime. Perhaps then people might realize that these criminals who have taken the lives of others have no right to live. We give too much consideration to the criminal. Let us give some consideration to those who are the sufferers, the victims of the criminals.

Mr. Speaker, I believe I had a few more minutes to go at five o'clock. I was talking about minority language rights when it came to education. But for a moment or two I should like to review what I said earlier. I started off by saying that this party thinks we have come to a time in history when we need a constitutional change in this country, and I said that later on in this debate other members would talk about the need for changes in a number of areas, one of them being changes with regard to our native Canadians, the original people, another one being the failure of the government to refer in this resolution to offshore resources. I spoke about the absolute necessity to have something in this resolution about resources. This is very important, not just to western Canada but indeed to all provinces in our country. Without the inclusion of resources, I want to make it very clear that I do not see this resolution supported by people in western Canada. That resource section is absolutely vital. I also said earlier that we have grave concerns about section 42
October 7, 1980

of the resolution. That is the part of the resolution where the federal Parliament can unilaterally hold a referendum on a constitutional matter in this country. Regardless of what a provincial legislature may do, regardless of whether or not in a provincial legislature all the parties are united in opposing a referendum, a referendum may be held and it may pass because the federal government is playing with loaded dice. They have control of the referendum question, they write the question, they determine the funds and they determine all the rules for that referendum. I find that to be highly unacceptable, as I said before the supper hour.
I also referred to the section on equalization and said that we agree in principle to equalization. But in the resolution before us today-and I wish hon. members would take a look at it-there is no reference at all to equalization payments. I find that absolutely disgusting and unacceptable. Under the formula, which only one province supported at the conference here a month ago, nine provinces argued for a different approach. I say we must change that to make sure that equalization payments are referred to and that a system such as the provinces want is included. There is a system that is talked about in here, one where the federal government can go over the heads of provincial governments and make payments directly to individuals in various provinces. That is not right and not fair and I find it very difficult to support that kind of approach.
The fourth point about which I was really concerned, and I was speaking about this in detail at five o'clock, arises in sections 20 and 23 dealing with official languages. As 1 said, in section 20 we are talking about the official languages as they pertain to the federal Parliament and to federal institutions. There is a reference here to the phrase "where numbers warrant", but it is the federal Parliament which is going to decide whether or not the numbers warrant it. But when one turns to section 23, one finds it talks about minority language educational rights and when we get to "where numbers warrant", all of a sudden there is a double standard and we see that it is not the provinces, with their control over education which will determine that, but it is the courts which will make that determination. I say this is not acceptable. It is not acceptable to have that double standard in federalism where, on the one hand, Parliament will make decisions which affect our institutions while, on the other hand, when it comes to the provinces, matters are left to the courts to decide.
1 wanted to refer very briefly to a communique which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is very fond of quoting. He quoted this communique last Thursday evening in the televised address to the people of this country. It is a February, 1978, communique from the premiers who met in Montreal when they spoke about language rights in education. They said:
The premiers reaffirm their intention to make their best efforts to provide education to their English or French-speaking minorities, and in order to ensure appropriate levels of services, they also agree that the following principles should govern the availability of, as well as accessibility to, such services;
(i) each child of the French-speaking or English-speaking minority is entitled
to an education in his or her language in the primary or the secondary schools
in each province wherever numbers warrant

That is what the Prime Minister refers to when he talks about all the premiers agreeing to this. But what he does not say is what is contained in the second part of the communique, which 1 think is very important. It reads:

There is a very important difference here and I suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) that he accept that principle because there are demographic differences in this country from one province to the other. Education is under the exclusive authority of the provincial governments, and if we are going to have Parliament define "where numbers warrant" in the case of federal bilingualism, we should make sure the same rights reside with the provincial legislatures, that they define where numbers warrant.

I have a number of concerns about the resolution before us. I suppose I am airing those concerns as a warning to the government. A lot has been written about the fact that the government has widespread support among its people for what it is doing. But within that support I detect a great deal of apprehension about a number of things in the resolution. I detect a great deal of apprehension in western Canada, Quebec, Newfoundland and among the original peoples of this country, just to name a few. Because those apprehensions are there, I have made four or five points today-a number of further points will be made by my colleagues later.
I mentioned original peoples and offshore resources. Those apprehensions are there because of the process which occurred over the summer and the fact that the government failed to widen the negotiating process as was suggested by my leader and the leader of the Conservative party last June. Also, the apprehension is there because of the advertising campaign launched by the government at a cost of $6 million over the course of the summer. Also it is there because the budget of the unity information office has been increased from $9 million or $10 million to around $33 million. We wonder what is to come.
In conclusion I should like to make one more suggestion to the government. It was contained in a resolution passed by my party on September 7. It was supported by my leader, my caucus and the national council of the party. It was a bit of advice for the government concerning future constitutional negotiations which we hope will be ongoing. I should like to read part of the resolution. After the September 8 to September 12 conference we recommended the following:
-that a new round of deliberations be started almost immediately and that the conference participants include multiparty delegations selected by Parliament and each of the provincial legislatures-

October 7, 1980
The Constitution
in addition, that the original peoples be given the right to direct representation and vote in the deliberations;
in addition, that multiparty delegations from the territories be given the right to direct representation and vote in the deliberations;
in addition, a delegation of women's organizations be given the right to direct representation and vote in the deliberations;
that a series of regional meetings be held by this group across Canada.
In effect this would bring the discussion on the constitution closer to the people of Canada. It is important to learn a few lessons from what has happened and to widen the negotiating process to include the government and the opposition here, the governments and the opposition parties of all legislatures, the legislatures of the two territories, the original peoples and women's organizations. In my opinion the constitution belongs to more than just 11 men. All the heads of government in this country happen to be men, and I am not sure that all the views of Canada with its divergent regions and people can be properly reflected in the process that has gone on until now.
I suggest to the government that we should broaden the process and that the process should be started as soon as possible. We should consider making serious changes to the resolution before us. We should dig out the repugnant section on the direct referendum to be organized solely and exclusively by the government. It strikes at the very essence of federalism. It can take away by referendum what has been given in a charter of rights in a time of emotional concern. We should entrench the philosophy of equalization payments so that there may be genuine equality of condition across the country. We should not have a double standard when it comes to federalism.
Sections 20 and 23 refer to the official languages, which is a very sensitive issue. If it is good enough for Parliament for us to define "where numbers warrant" concerning our institutions, programs and things we do, then surely in the name of equity, co-operative federalism and fairness, it is for the provinces to define "where numbers warrant" when it comes to education in minority languages rather than leaving it to the courts.
Finally changes are absolutely necessary in the area of resources so that there may be access to indirect taxation, concurrent powers with the provinces in international and interprovincial trade with federal paramountcy because it is international and interprovincial. There must be a clarification of resource ownership. 1 appeal to the government to seek such a consensus, to listen to all members of Parliament and indeed to some of its own backbenchers, some of whom are not happy at all with a number of matters in the resolution before us. I appeal to the government to listen to the people of Canada, the various provincial political parties both government and opposition from one coast to the other. If the government does this, perhaps it will be a very historic beginning, the beginning of a new Canada, not the end, or something which will turn out to be a very tragic nightmare.
I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) running out. I hope he heeds our words and makes some very serious changes to this resolution. If he does I assure him all Canada will applaud.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to follow such a distinguished member of the House as the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), particularly after the remarks he made in closing when he indicated how important he thought it was to the country and its people that this Parliament be the focal point for this debate.
There is a certain moment in each decade and generation when events begin to converge and Parliament becomes the centre of the nation. In the past many commentators have assessed that Parliament is no longer the power it once was, that it is the executive, the cabinet, which is the centre of influence. Some have even suggested that there is a new level of government in Canada called the federal-provincial conference which makes the real decisions about how we are to be governed. I believe this debate once again shows how relevant and valuable an institution Parliament is. I for one am very glad that the debate has finally come to its proper home. The debate about the constitutional laws of this country is now outside the arena of the federal-provincial conference and in an arena where the full range of opinions and views in all regions can be heard, expressed, debated and discussed.
In the end, this is the place where the choice should be made. It should not be made around a table by 11 people who, though they represent regions, do not in any way represent the full range of opinions and views withtin those regions. As one of the western members on the government benches, I think it is very important that I express this other point of view which 1, together with hundreds of thousands of western Canadians believe, was not expressed at the federal-provincial conference last September.

woe-betide-the-country, that this will devour the nation, that this will be the downfall of Canadian democracy. That is the myth. That is the great Tory lie in this country. That is the great Tory mythology which they have spread up and down this country. Why? Because they cannot use logic, they cannot use reason, they cannot use rationality. So what do they use? They use personality assassination. That is the nature of their attack. It is an interesting comment, you can always tell when the other side does not have an argument because that is when they start picking on people. It goes right back to schoolyard politics and battles. If you really do not have a basis of reason and rationality, what do you do? You pick on the person. We have found out that this art has been developed to a fine form by members over there, because they do not have much reason, much rationality or logic in their position.
Thus we hear the Premier of Manitoba and other members from the opposition saying that a bill of rights is unCanadian, that a bill of rights is really going to destroy the fundamental traditions of our country, that we should adhere to the British system of common law. 1 am sure hon. members would be interested in the September 22 copy of the Manchester Guardian I have here. It says Lord Hailsham and Sir Keith Joseph and all the members of the Margaret Thatcher government are doing two things: one, they are considering a new charter of rights for the British Parliament and, two, they have just ratified the European Convention of Human Rights. I

I would suggest they read what their counterparts in Great Britain are talking about. Why? Because even the Thatcher government recognizes and understands that when the country becomes complex and pluralistic there must be some fundamental set of rights as a standard by which people can determine what their guarantees and protections are.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: They say the bill of rights is something which is foreign to our traditions because we are afraid of the courts; we cannot go to the courts. They say we should depend on the legislatures.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: They are unreliable.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Maybe they are unreliable but we use them every day. What about the Bliss case, the Lavallee case and the Drybones case, all the cases being judged by our courts every single day dealing with questions of human rights? The weakness in their argument is that there is not a bill of rights upon which the courts can properly decide. The Canadian Bill of Rights which was passed in this House in the early sixties is not strong enough and the Supreme Court decisions have said that they need further guidance from this Parliament on the constitution in order to establish a common standard of rights across Canada. That is why we do need a bill of rights-not only to make sure there is an evenness and equality in those opportunities and rights, but it is also needed to set directions for the courts in the decisions they are making every single day dealing with matters of human rights in this country. There is nothing untraditional or uncommon about the courts dealing in these matters.
Then we come to the argument that I have heard Mr. Lyon use. He says we should trust the legislatures, trust the legislature of Manitoba. But I ask you, Mr. Speaker, did George Forrest trust the legislature of Manitoba to get his rights as a French-speaking Manitoban guaranteed? No. He had to go to traffic court to get his rights guaranteed. 1 was a member of that legislature for several years and I was there when a resolution was initiated by our party, and rejected by the other parties, trying to establish some basic fundamental rights.
The legislature of Manitoba spoke so well to the issue of linguistic rights in that province, that Mr. Forrest had to go to a traffic court to have his rights protected because our legislature was not prepared to deal with these rights.

majority. It does not matter what party is in power in which legislature. This is why we need a fundamental charter.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: If you are going to lecture about logic, I suggest you listen to your own rhetoric.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
There are many people in western Canada who feel, because we are the most multicultural society and the most pluralistic region in the country, that it is absolutely essential that we have a bill of rights. This fact has not been expressed by western members or western premiers. In fact there is an increase in discrimination against the new ethnic groups moving into the west. In a recent study by a social scientist from Alberta, of all places, it was shown that discrimination was on the increase during the 1970s and that ethnic groups themselves are far more concerned about such fundamental protection, protection which they want.
So there are many people in the west who want a bill of rights. There are many people in western Canada who feel it is important that it be entrenched in the constitution. They do not buy the great conspiracy theory which says that somehow it is all unparliamentary or unCanadian to include such a charter of rights in our constitution. In fact they feel it is the best way of enhancing our fundamental freedoms, rights and liberties, and they are prepared when the chips come down to back us on this particular issue.
Let us deal with another one of the great myths about which I have heard the provincial premiers and their spokesmen in this House, the Leader of the Opposition, talk, that somehow this is all a federal plot to pick on those poor, weak, defenceless provinces of the west, those poor provinces which are struggling to survive. That just does not conform to reality because the fact of the matter is that for the last ten or 15 years of this confederation powers have been devolving rapidly to the provinces and the fact of the matter is that the provinces have by far the largest expenditures from the public purse. They make close to 50 per cent of the public expenditures in this country, 15 per cent more than what is spent by the federal government. If those trends continue, the ratio will be 75/25 in ten years' time.
The provinces are not defenceless and weak, but in fact are very powerful. At the present moment, our federation is probably the weakest and most decentralized of any federal system in the world. The reality we must face is that if we intend to manage and deal with the conditions and issues we must face in this decade, then we need a far more effective central government to provide that effective management and growth.
The fact of the matter is these powerful provincial premiers do not want change. Of course they do not want change. They want the status quo, because they have the chips on their side.
October 7, 1980

Why would they deal away a winning hand. What we are talking about, of course, is a power play or a power game being played by the provincial premiers and, of course, they will stand up on their hind legs and rear because they do not want to share any of their powers. It is far more important to them in their political mandates to amass more power and more influence. The question arises, though, whether this is good for the country. Is this really what is necessary at the present time having regard to the problems and conditions that we will face in this decade?
I am here as a western Canadian saying, "No, it is not what we need". If we allow devolution to continue and decentralization to take place, then we as western Canadians will have given away one of the great opportunities in this country to help our region grow. The fundamental assumption which is being made by members of both the Conservative party and the New Democratic Party is that it is only the provinces which can manage this new growth in western Canada, that it is only the provinces and provincial jurisdictions which should be the managers of the new wealth.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Who said that?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I do not have time to name all of you. The fact is that we did offer concessions to the provinces. This seems to have been conveniently forgotten among the hysteria and exaggeration implying that somehow there is a Liberal conspiracy to destroy the provinces. I saw the list of concessions which was assembled for the constitutional conference. We were prepared to share the powers of taxation with the provinces on resources. We were prepared to share interprovincial trade and powers over communications and fisheries. Where was the conspiracy against the provinces in those concessions?
However, Mr. Speaker, if one looks at the other side of the ledger at what those generous, open-hearted visionary provinces were offering, it adds up to one big goose egg. They were playing the game of "heads 1 win, tails you lose". It was a classic no-bargain, no-win game. The federal government would have betrayed its fundamental mandate if we had even listened to that kind of blackmail. We went into those conferences with all the right intentions to bargain and to share and to deal with the provinces, but we did not get anything in return.
What we must really examine at this point, because I believe it is important to the debate, is really what kind of federal state is necessary to take advantage and develop the new-found opportunities of western Canada. There has been historically and is a strong and abiding role for the federal government, but this has been conveniently forgotten by hon. members opposite. When the prairies were in trouble during the depression, it was the federal government which moved in with the wheat board, the PFRA and other kinds of grain acts. It was the federal government which used its declaratory
The Constitution
powers to bring in the Wheat Board in order to protect the western farmer. Those are the very powers we are being asked to give away at the present time.
It embarrasses me at times to hear the kind of expressions which come from certain western politicians, including the premier of my province, who has no business saying what he says because we are a have-not province. We need equalization, not him saying, "Now that we have ours, we are going to keep it". Suddenly equalization, which was one of the basic touchstones for western Canada for many years, can be conveniently forgotten because we have discovered a big pool of oil and gas below our soil.
This kind of spirit in western Canada is not the kind of traditional spirit of which I feel a part. It may be the tradition which has been there historically, a kind of New Englander approach-how to shrink your horizons, in your dimensions and draw yourself into a fetal position for utmost protection. That is not the only point of view that is being heard in the west. There are many westerners who say they would like to share and the only vehicle and mechanism for that sharing is the federal government. That sharing must be in our interest as westerners as well as in the interests of the entire country.
In the next decade we will go through an amazing growth in the west. We will be putting billions of dollars into railroads, water systems, research and development and industrialization. By their nature there must be some degree of crossregional management in these areas.

speechtext: I hear a harrumph from the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). I am glad he has finally come awake in this debate. The fact is we must recognize the realities, not dreams and fantasies. Let me use an example from my own department.

I have made that speech in Winnipeg five times in the past two weeks. I am going to the hon. member's province on Thursday to make it again, and he is invited to come. In fact, I will be glad to accept an invitation from the hon. member to speak at his next riding association meeting. They might find it educational.
Let us look at one dimension that concerns my ministerial responsibilities, namely, the enormous movement of people, both within and outside the region in western Canada. We are talking about the need to develop 30,000 or 40,000 skilled jobs per year for western Canada. We are talking about training hundreds of thousands of people over the next decade to do the work that is necessary to ensure the growth of the west. We are talking about trying to make sure that this enormous employment opportunity is available to the native people of western Canada and to women in this country. We are talking about using the enormous growth potential that exists.

When I start negotiating how to provide these skills and this training I find, increasingly, provincial barriers to the movement of labour or certification laws which provide that people cannot work in a certain place because they do not have a white piece of paper-their paper is not the right colour. When we try to sign training agreements with industries in western Canada, right away the provincial governments say we cannot have training agreements with their industries. When we talk about introducing affirmative action programs to make sure there is equal opportunity for native people, the provincial governments tell us they do not believe in affirmative action. They claim there is no inequality in their provinces and they do not have affirmative actions, and therefore the agreement cannot be signed.
Our capacity and ability to provide some degree of management of the human resources which are absolutely essential for the development of the west, are being hindered and handicapped by the increasing growth of provincial barriers to the mobility and movement of people. They are being hindered and handicapped by the increasing number of labour laws and provincial human rights codes which prevent federal activity providing those skills and opportunities. We cannot build the west with those kinds of barriers, Mr. Speaker. We cannot fulfil our destiny unless there is some jurisdiction that provides comprehensive management. The people must come from somewhere. They cannot come from under the ground like the oil and gas. They must come from other parts of Canada or from offshore and someone has to manage that movement. That is one of the great tasks of our time.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

The federal government is doing it right now because the provinces are not prepared to or are not in a position to.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Let us now talk about resource management-all right, we will cut off all the grants in your provinces and see how much they are going to react in Ottawa! If you think it is a big handicap, we will see. We will call your bluff on that one.
Let us talk about resource management. We hear a great deal about the provincial premiers and how they want to make sure they can manage the oil and gas and the coal and the electricity. What we do not hear about them is how they are going to manage the forests or the farms in those areas. It is a fact that the condition of the soil in the west is deteriorating every year and that there is no reforestation being done in western Canada. Those resources are under provincial management and lie within their jurisdiction. Somehow they have forgotten about resource management. Why? Because there are not as many bucks in those areas as there are in others. What is happening now is that every day coal is being mined. The Minister of DREE and the minister responsible for forestry have applications on their desks asking them to look after the fisheries or the forests or the farms. When they get into trouble they know where the first hand is out-it is the provincial hand out for the federal purse.
That is the way federalism should work, Mr. Speaker. We must recognize, however, that in order to provide that kind of management and control, we need to share in some of the revenues from those resources. We simply cannot be drawing purely upon a tax base which is static and that is a part of what the debate is about. That is why we have to work at changing the rules and why we have to ensure that there is at least an equal sharing of powers over the resources of this country. There is no ambition whatsoever to intervene in existing powers over resources. There is not a line in the resolution that says we are going to take resource powers away from the provinces.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) made a revelation on Monday. We were very pleased with his constructive comments but he said we forgot the whole question of the provision of powers over resources. We did not forget it, Mr. Speaker; we altered it. We altered it at the conference. It was not forgotten; it was there on the table for the provinces to pick up. They did not pick it up, however, Mr. Speaker. We offered to provide some of our share.

The hon. member should have opened up earlier. We feel that the issue on the division of powers should still be discussed and debated and negotiated.
There is no point getting into that debate, however, until we have in this Parliament and in our own hands the ability to make changes to our constitution. The history of constitutional change in Canada has been that every time we reach a consensus or agreement and are ready to make a change, we do not have the lever because it is in England. By the time we figure out how to get it, the consensus has changed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

We also consider a debate on resources to be an important debate, it is something that should be looked at as part of constitutional change. It is a critical item in terms of where we go in this country and it is something we have to put in place in this constitution. But other things must come first. We must obtain the power to make the amendments in our own constitution so that when some of those provincial governments change-as the government of Manitoba will change next year and the government of British Columbia the year after and several others-we may get a more progressive point of view from those provinces, allowing us to get back into serious, sharing negotiations. Then we can bring about the

changes we need because we will have the power in Canada to make those changes when we need them.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very pleased indeed to answer the hon. member's question.
I think we have seen that a number of myths have been perpetrated and a number of fantasies have been spread around this House and other places about what the west really wants. I think it is time we dispelled those myths and realized there is just as much a commitment among western Canadians to the position stated in this resolution as there is in other regions of Canada.
Evidence of this is supplied to me daily from western Canada. Just this week someone told me he did not realize how much of a federalist he was until he heard the premiers speak. Westerners are really saying that they are prepared to make the federalist choice-to make a choice in terms of what they see as a necessity for their own region to develop through strong, effective, central government and to use that strong, effective, central government to provide some degree of sharing of its resources and its opportunities with other Canadians.
There are also westerners who have not given up on the ideal of equalization. They still believe this country is based upon the notion of equality of opportunity and they are not prepared to abandon that.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Hon. members opposite say that is not so, Mr. Speaker. 1 do not know what conference they were watching in September. If there is all the agreement with equalization and bills of rights and repatriation that hon. members opposite have indicated, why are they opposing this resolution? If there is all that agreement, then why are they opposing it? Do they have principles or do they not? Do they believe in what they say or do they not? If they say they agree with all those items, then why do we do not have the vote tonight, get the resolution passed and go to England as soon as possible? What are we waiting for, if there is this consensus and agreement? Are they simply interested in using this debate for some degree of political posturing?
I suspect there is no problem of unity in Canada, Mr. Speaker. But there is a problem of unity in the Tory caucus. They do not know what they believe in and they do not know where they belong, because there is no agreement among members of that caucus. Their only tactic is to attack. Let them state what they believe in. I would be very interested in hearing them. What kind of constitution do they want? They have been very good at saying what they are against, but what are they for?
The Constitution
There is a line in the play "The Rainmaker". When the evangelical preacher is on his feet holding forth, someone tells him he is so busy being right, he forgets what is good. 1 suggest that hon. members opposite are so busy being right that they forget what is good for this country.
Finally, it comes down to the fact that this is not a debate between the federal government and the provincial governments. Governments are simply a means to an end. They are simply mechanisms for achieving goals and values for people. They are simply a way of trying to provide basic values for what we want to achieve in this country. Rather than degrading this debate into a great federal-provincial clash, what we should be talking about is what it means for the individuals of this country. What does it mean for people in this country? What will this resolution do for women who have been denied their rights for many, many years in this country? How will the entrenchment of a bill of rights make sure that when they go to court to get equality or when they try to get a proper definition of their rights before the courts they will have some protection under the law?
What does it mean for individuals in this country who want to make sure they can work wherever they live, because they are Canadian, and are not disbarred from working simply because they do not happen to be an inhabitant of one province or another. There are many people who want to see in our constitution not some abstract piece of theory, not something politicians just talk about, but the real nuts and bolts of their daily lives. It means restructuring our foundations so that we will have the powers to begin to provide for the effective management and growth of our economy.
There was an interesting sort of trio who all agreed that the federal government at the present time does not have enough power nor does it have the levers required to do the job it has to do, namely, the economic council, Joe Clark and Jacques Parizeau. None of those can be considered to be a Liberal adherent, from what 1 can tell, yet they all agreed the federal government at this point does not have the ability to govern and manage in the way it should. I agree with those statements and that is why we need to go back to some fundamentals as to how we change our constitution. 1 think, Mr. Speaker, we should ask that question about what kind of government can best serve the demands and needs and necessities of Canadians over the next several decades and get away from the picayune technicalities, which we can deal with in committee, and come back to some fundamental questions on the principles of constitutional change. If we can do so, I think this Parliament will have served very well its purpose of helping this country to make a choice about how it is going to govern itself in the future, and how it will provide a framework of government to give it the ability to be the kind of country we all want it to be.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must admit that this debate is of great interest and significance.
